figures.bridge_line: The church at Rome, writing as one church to another. The letter names no individual author.

dates.display: the letter is traditionally dated c. 96; the plausible range is broadened by current scholarship to 80-140

names.name: the church of God sojourning at Rome
the Roman church as collective author of 1 Clement (traditional attribution to Clement of Rome is not self-declared in the text)

figures.bridge_line: The church at Smyrna, telling the death of its own teacher in a letter to another church.

dates.display: writing after Polycarp's death (c. 155-156 traditional; 167 per the Chronicon); the closing chapters are widely regarded as later additions

names.name: the church of God sojourning at Smyrna
the Smyrnaean community as collective author of the Martyrdom of Polycarp

figures.bridge_line: A freedman in Rome who wrote down his own visions - about failure, doubt, and whether mercy is used up.

dates.display: the Shepherd was composed c. 90-150, possibly in stages
dates.note: these bound the WORK, not the man - his own dates are not attested

names.name: Hermas
Hermas (the Shepherd of Hermas, Rome)

figures.bridge_line: A bishop of Antioch, taken under guard to Rome to die. Seven of his letters survive.

dates.display: the letters are traditionally dated c. 107-117; one scholarly camp redates them to the 130s-140s, another holds them pseudepigraphic compositions of c. 160-180
dates.note: deliberately no single year: the three positions are not a range, and collapsing them would settle in a data field the dispute every telling must carry. These bound the LETTERS, not the man's life.

names.name: Ignatius, bishop of Antioch
Ignatius of Antioch (the middle-recension letters; authenticity and dating three-way split)

figures.bridge_line: A philosopher who kept the philosopher's dress after becoming a Christian. He described our Sunday worship in an open letter to the emperor, and died for the name he defended.

dates.display: First Apology c. 153-157; died c. 165 - the best-anchored dating in this world's whole source set

names.name: Justin
Justin Martyr (First Apology c. 153-157, Dialogue with Trypho before his death c. 165, per Minns and Parvis)

figures.bridge_line: Two enslaved women who served their church in some named way, and were tortured by a governor for what they knew. Their names, their words, and their lives were not kept.

dates.display: interrogated under torture in Bithynia-Pontus, c. 111-113

names.name: the two enslaved women tortured by Pliny, called ministrae in his letter (unnamed; the title is Latin, the outside report's word - no in-world name or self-designation survives)

figures.bridge_line: The scattered assemblies themselves - households, letters, couriers - speaking as communities where no individual author is named.

names.name: the churches in correspondence - the ekklesiai themselves
the post-apostolic house-church network (composite communal owner for anonymous and typical-practice material)

figures.bridge_line: A bishop in Asia who collected what the elders remembered of the apostles - because he trusted a living voice over books. His own books are lost.

dates.display: active in Hierapolis of Asia in the early second century; the dating of his writing is itself disputed among scholars (earlier and later placements are both live) and is not settled here
dates.note: deliberately no year range: the fragments' own transmission gives no secure anchor, and the record set's dates-field discipline does not collapse live disputes into data fields. These concern the man's activity as later writers report it; his own life-dates are unattested.

names.name: Papias of Hierapolis
Papias (fragments only, preserved in Irenaeus and Eusebius; his own five books are lost)

figures.bridge_line: A Roman governor, not a Christian. He questioned Christians under threat of death, tortured two enslaved women for details, and wrote to the emperor asking what the rules were.

dates.display: c. 61-c. 113 (standard reference dates, not from this world's own record); governor of Bithynia-Pontus c. 111-113, when the letters were written

names.name: Pliny, the emperor's governor in Bithynia
Pliny the Younger (Gaius Plinius Caecilius Secundus, c. 61-c. 113; Letters 10.96-97, c. 111-113)

figures.bridge_line: A church leader at Smyrna, burned in the arena for refusing to curse Christ. His own letter survives.

dates.died: c. 155-156 (traditional) or 167 (Chronicon) - both carried, neither forced
dates.display: martyred c. 155-156 by the traditional dating; Eusebius's Chronicon gives 167

names.name: Polycarp of Smyrna
Polycarp (Letter to the Philippians; the Martyrdom of Polycarp)

figures.bridge_line: A Roman historian, not a Christian. He recorded Nero blaming Christians for the great fire - with open contempt for them and for Nero alike.

dates.display: c. 56-c. 120 (standard reference dates, not from this world's own record); the Annals passage written c. 116, describing 64

names.name: Tacitus, the Roman historian
Tacitus (Annals 15.44, written c. 116 about the events of 64)
